canonical_statement: The study examined characteristics associated with abandonment of newly prescribed buprenorphine for opioid use disorder and trends in first-prescription abandonment from 2020 through 2024.

The study was a retrospective cohort analysis of deidentified electronic health record data linked to administrative claims from the Optum Labs Data Warehouse; claims represented commercial and Medicare Advantage enrollees and EHR data represented participating US health care groups and organizations.

Eligible patients were adults aged 18 years or older with a first prescribed buprenorphine prescription for opioid use disorder between January 1, 2020 and September 25, 2024, with continuous medical and pharmacy benefit enrollment for at least 180 days before and 30 days after the index date, allowing a coverage gap of 45 days or less.

canonical_statement: Buprenorphine prescription abandonment was defined as no dispensing or filling record for the first prescribed buprenorphine within 30 days of the index date, including prescriptions not filled by patients or rejected by insurers or pharmacies.

outcome.definition: No dispensing or filling record for the first prescribed buprenorphine within 30 days of the index date, including patient non-fill or insurer/pharmacy rejection

canonical_statement: Characteristics were compared between patients with dispensed and abandoned prescriptions using t tests for continuous variables and Pearson chi-square tests for categorical variables.

A weighted least-squares regression tested the linear trend in yearly first-prescription abandonment proportions from 2020 through 2024; two-sided P values below .05 were considered statistically significant.
The final cohort included 1428 patients; mean age was 56.6 years, 50.6% were male, 7.9% were Black, 6.3% were Hispanic, and 84.0% were White.

canonical_statement: Patients with abandoned prescriptions were younger than those whose prescriptions were dispensed: mean age 54.3 vs 57.4 years (P=.001).
Hispanic ethnicity was more frequent among patients with abandoned prescriptions than among those dispensed buprenorphine: 10.6% vs 4.8% (P=.003).
Commercial insurance was more frequent among patients with abandoned prescriptions than among those dispensed buprenorphine: 51.8% vs 29.4% (P<.001).
Mean pharmacy deductibles were higher among patients with abandoned prescriptions than among those dispensed buprenorphine: $483.80 vs $296.40 (P=.006).
An opioid use disorder or overdose diagnosis in the prior 180 days was less frequent among patients with abandoned prescriptions than among those dispensed buprenorphine: 40.1% vs 54.4% (P<.001).
Another substance use disorder diagnosis in the prior 180 days was less frequent among patients with abandoned prescriptions than among those dispensed buprenorphine: 15.5% vs 21.0% (P=.02).

canonical_statement: A mental health diagnosis in the prior 180 days was less frequent among patients with abandoned prescriptions than among those dispensed buprenorphine: 38.5% vs 52.5% (P<.001).
The study identified no statistically significant between-group differences in sex, race, or tier-2 retail pharmacy copay.
The yearly proportion of first buprenorphine prescriptions abandoned increased from 19% in 2020 to 37% in 2024, with P for trend=.02.

canonical_statement: The authors characterized the increase in abandonment through 2024, when more than 1 in 3 first prescriptions were abandoned, as a missed opportunity for treatment initiation and engagement.
The authors proposed that the higher abandonment proportion among Hispanic patients might reflect language and pharmacy-level access barriers; the study did not directly test those mechanisms.

The authors suggested that pharmacy plan deductibles may be associated with abandonment and stated that the higher abandonment proportion among commercial vs Medicare Advantage enrollees warrants further analysis of insurance benefit design, including prior authorization, quantity limits, and cost-sharing.
The authors stated that direct buprenorphine dispensing during clinical encounters, stronger linkage to care, and improved pharmacy availability could help reduce treatment-access barriers.
The authors stated that findings may have limited generalizability beyond people with commercial insurance or Medicare Advantage.
The study could not distinguish prescriptions that patients did not fill from prescriptions rejected by insurers or pharmacies.
Abandonment could be misclassified when prescriptions were paid with cash, assistance programs, or other insurance not captured in the linked claims data.
The reported characteristic comparisons were bivariate and the article did not report a multivariable model estimating independent predictors of prescription abandonment.
The article reported no conflicts of interest.
